items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: "he had proposed these musicians plus 'Big Boy' Goddie and myself and the owner had accepted the proposition."

ctx.x: Michel de Villers had learned a lot from Charlie Parker records, and played the style well. His only draw back was that he didn't read music. Geo Daly was considered the Lionel Hampton of France. He and Peiffer did a Hamp and Milt Buckner act on the piano with Geo (pronounced Gee-o) doing the one finger bit like Hamp, and that always pleased the audiance. Jean Bouchety was a fine bass fiddle man, arranger and pilot. But I never knew if he had flown a plane during the war. Roger Paraboschi played solid drums which…

Eventually, I ran into "Big Boy" Goddie, who had spent the 2nd world war years in South America. I also later saw Arthur Briggs, who had been in a concentration camp after the Germans occupied Paris. Briggs told me why the few of the old gang that was still in Parid did not hang around in Boudon's anymore. The owner had collaborated with the Germans, and had denounced some Jews and Negros. I had been eating in the place, but went somewhere else after hearing what Briggs told me.

I heard that Rex Stewart was in Paris, but didn't see him until two weeks had passed as I didn't know where he was living, I happened to be sitting at the Omnibus café at Place Pigalle, and Rex came alone. He had come to Europe in 1947 with a group that included Sandy Williams, ex-Chick Webb trombonist, Vernon Story, a tenor sax man. Don Gais, piano, Johnny Harris, alto and clarinet, Ted Curry, drums and Honey Johnson, a vocalist. He used an unknown French bassist.
